newsitem.title: BELGIUM: SGB still wants G-Bank, BBL merger.
newsitem.headline: SGB still wants G-Bank, BBL merger.

text.p: Philippe Liotier, chief executive officer of Belgian holding company Societe Generale de Belgique (SGB), said he is still interested in a merger between SGB unit Generale Bank and Banque Bruxelles Lambert (BBL).
"We are interested in a merger between Generale Bank and BBL, but not at any cost," Liotier was quoted as saying in the magazine of Flemish Investment Club Federation VFB.
In January, SGB Chairman Etienne Davignon also said he still thought a BBL-Generale Bank merger was a good business idea.

Just last week Michel Tilmant, BBL's new CEO since January, said that he saw his bank's future in a "stand-alone" perspective. But at the same time he indicated that a BBL-Generale Bank merger could not be ruled out.

Early last year SGB floated for the first time the idea of a merger between the two banks but later said that the project had been blocked by opposition from Dutch banking and insurance group Internationale Nederlanden Groep (ING).
ING controls 20 percent of BBL shares, following a failed hostile takeover bid for BBL five years ago.

"Our intention was to create a new entity which would be bigger in Belgium and which would have more funds to grow internationally, in short: a large Belgian international bank," Liotier was quoted as saying.

"ING, however, wanted to hold a 20 percent stake in the new entity, as it now has in BBL, and that was the problem. ING is already strong on the international level and is primarily interested in Belgium. Thus, there was a risk of conflicts of interest and decisions which could damage the new entity, which we as most important shareholder cannot accept," Liotier said. These were SGB's first specific comments on the failed merger.

Liotier said that he saw no synergies between SGB's insurance unit Fortis AG and Generale Bank. Some investors have seen a merger of the two as a possibility, because of the success of the banking-insurance concept within other groups.
Liotier, a 65-year-old Frenchman, represents French Compagnie de Suez which holds 62.6 percent of SGB.
